newsitem.title: JAPAN: N.Korea demands apology for border incident.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea demands apology for border incident.

text.p: North Korea demanded on Friday that South Korea apologise for endangering its troops' lives during an exchange of shots at their tense border shortly before U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen visited the area.

Seoul officials said that in the incident, on Thursday, South Korean troops in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) fired 10 warning shots after spotting a group of North Korean soldiers who had crossed the border. North Korean troops returned fire.

"South Korea should apologise for having obstructed the normal patrol work of the (North Korean) People's Army and endangered their lives and they should take steps that this will never happen again," official North Korean radio broadcasts monitored in Tokyo said.

"The reason this incident did not break out into a military clash between both parties is due entirely to the perseverance and restraint of our men in the People's Army, who sought to avoid raising tensions at the DMZ," Pyongyang Radio said.
The incident happened about one hour before Cohen visited an area of the DMZ about 100 km (60 miles) west of where the exchange of fire occurred.
"We cannot ignore the fact that this is repeatedly happening just when the head of the U.S. military (Cohen) is being induced by South Korea into their plans to invade the North," it added.
Cohen told reporters the shooting incident "confirms that it is still a very tense, dangerous, unstable situation as far as the North Koreans are concerned".

Earlier this week, North Korea attacked Cohen for saying that virtually all of the 37,000 U.S. troops in South Korea would remain there for the foreseeable future, even if the Koreas made peace and were united.
The shooting incident happened ahead of an expected North Korean response next week to a U.S.-South Korea proposal for peace talks also involving China.

The United States and South Korea proposed the four-party talks on April 19, 1996, as a way to defuse tensions on the Korean peninsula and get to a peace treaty that would finally close the books on the 1950-53 war that divided the peninsula.
